      • 15. Subgroups, cosets, and Lagrange’s theorem

      15. Subgroups, cosets, and Lagrange’s theorem#

      The rotations of the square form a group with elements, sitting inside the group of all symmetries. The two symmetries and also form a group by themselves. Could some symmetries of the square form a group? Could a symmetry of the square have order ? Questions of this kind ask how the size of a group restricts the groups and the elements inside it. This note answers them by splitting a group into blocks of equal size, called cosets, and then counting with the division rule from Unit I. The result is Lagrange’s theorem: the order of a group inside a finite group divides . Cosets will appear again in Lecture Note 16, where they explain why the number of colorings equivalent to a given coloring divides the order of the group.

      After studying these notes, you will be able to do the following.

      • Decide whether a subset of a group is a subgroup, and list the subgroups of a small group.

      • Compute the cyclic subgroup generated by a permutation and relate its size to the order of the permutation.

      • Compute the cosets of a subgroup and explain why they have equal sizes and do not overlap.

      • State and prove Lagrange’s theorem, and use it to rule out subgroup sizes and element orders.

      Throughout, is a group of permutations of a finite set , as defined in Lecture Note 14, and we write for the composition in which is applied first.

      15.3 Lagrange’s theorem#

      Counting the elements of block by block now gives the relation between and .

      Theorem 10 (Lagrange’s theorem)#

      Let be a subgroup of a finite group , and let be the number of different cosets of in . Then In particular, divides .

      Proof#

      The different cosets of are disjoint and together contain every element of , so by the sum rule is the sum of their sizes. Each of the cosets has elements, so .

      The number is called the index of in . The proof is an instance of the division rule: the elements of fall into blocks of exactly elements, so the number of blocks is . The division rule required every outcome to be represented the same number of times, and Lemma 8 is exactly that requirement for cosets.
